brand.subtitle: Knowledge Check — Introduction to Social Selling Techniques

questions.question: What are the two axes that form the foundation of the Social Style framework?
choices: Introversion vs. Extroversion and Planning vs. Spontaneity
Ask vs. Tell and Task vs. People
Speed vs. Accuracy and Logic vs. Emotion
Control vs. Collaboration and Results vs. Relationships
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—the entire model rests on how someone gets what they want (Ask vs. Tell) and what drives their behavior (Task vs. People).
questions.feedback_incorrect: The framework uses two specific axes that describe observable behavior. Review Slide 5 to see how Ask vs. Tell and Task vs. People create the four-quadrant grid.

questions.question: Which of the following is a signature question a Driver tends to ask?
choices: How does this work and how accurate is it?
Why should I choose this solution?
What are the results and what is the outcome?
Who else is using this and who is involved?
questions.feedback_correct: Drivers lead with "What?"—focused on outcomes, results, and what this gets them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Each style has a distinctive signature question. Drivers ask "What?", Analyticals ask "How?", Amiables ask "Why?", and Expressives ask "Who?". Review Slide 11 for the full breakdown.

questions.question: What emotional level do both Drivers and Analyticals typically display?
choices: High emotion and animated
Low emotion and controlled
Variable depending on the situation
Warm and soft-spoken
questions.feedback_correct: Both task-focused styles run low on visible emotion, which is why they can initially look similar—but the tell vs. ask instinct separates them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Both Drivers and Analyticals share the task-focus, which typically shows up as lower visible emotion. The real difference between them is that Drivers tell and Analyticals ask. Review Slide 9 for clarity.

questions.question: What is an Amiable's primary pressure behavior when a conversation goes off track?
choices: Takes control of the meeting
Asks for more time and more data
Becomes argumentative
Goes quiet and withdraws
questions.feedback_correct: When Amiables feel pressure or conflict, they withdraw rather than push back—that quiet withdrawal is their signature pressure behavior.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Each style has a distinct pressure behavior. Amiables tend to go quiet and withdraw when uncomfortable. Understanding these signals helps you catch and recover from style mismatches early. See Slide 12 for all four pressure behaviors.

questions.question: According to the course, what does versatility actually mean in the context of Social Style Selling?
choices: Being equally likable to all four buyer styles
Deliberately adjusting how you communicate so the buyer doesn't have to work as hard to connect with you
Adopting a completely different personality for each buyer type
Being flexible and agreeable in all situations
questions.feedback_correct: Versatility is a conscious adjustment that removes friction and helps buyers feel understood—not about pretending to be someone else.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Versatility is not about personality change or being more agreeable. It's a deliberate communication adjustment that helps buyers understand you better. This is a tangible commercial skill, not a personality trait. Review Slide 21.

questions.question: What should you do first when preparing a sales call with an Analytical buyer?
choices: Build rapport by focusing on personal details and shared interests
Lead with conclusions and results to capture their attention quickly
Prepare detailed, logical questions and gather evidence throughout
Ask curiosity questions and let them elaborate on their vision
questions.feedback_correct: Analyticals need rigor and evidence—preparing detailed questions and supporting your approach with data shows respect for their need for accuracy.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Analyticals are driven by accuracy, logic, and data. They need to feel the process is thorough and that you won't cut corners. Review Slide 16 to see the specific tactics that work with this style.

questions.question: If a buyer is warm and emotionally open but drawing you out with questions rather than holding the floor, which style are they most likely to be?
choices: Driver
Analytical
Amiable
Expressive
questions.feedback_correct: Amiables are warm and emotionally open but soft-spoken and focused on drawing others in through questions and listening—not holding the spotlight.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Amiables are warm with high emotion but ask questions and draw you out; Expressives are animated and hold the floor with storytelling. The tell vs. ask instinct is the key separator between these two people-focused styles. Review Slide 10.

questions.question: What is the relationship between someone's primary Social Style and their adjacent style?
choices: The adjacent style is used only in stressful situations
The adjacent style sits next to the primary on the grid and softens or modifies how the primary style shows up in real behavior
They are completely unrelated and don't interact with each other
The adjacent style determines the person's personality type
questions.feedback_correct: The adjacent style—sitting in the neighboring quadrant—explains mixed signals and why a buyer might not feel like a pure style.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Adjacent styles are located next to the primary style on the grid and influence behavior. For example, a Driver with an Expressive adjacent will be direct but warmer than a pure Driver. This explains why buyers sometimes send mixed signals. See Slide 13.

questions.question: Based on the research cited in the course, what percentage of sales reps who learned to read and adjust to Social Style closed sales they otherwise might not have closed?
choices: 92 percent
87 percent
79 percent
58 percent
questions.feedback_correct: That 58 percent figure represents real, additional revenue—sales that would not have happened without style awareness and adjustment.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course cites several impact statistics. The 58 percent figure represents reps who closed sales they otherwise might not have closed. The other percentages refer to different outcomes like relationship quality and influence. Review Slide 3 for the complete data.

questions.question: When you notice a sudden drop in buyer engagement—shorter answers, less eye contact, or a shift in body language—what should you recognize this as?
choices: A sign that the buyer is not interested in your solution
Normal variation in buyer mood and attention
An early warning signal of a style mismatch that you still have time to correct
A cue that you need to push harder with your pitch
questions.feedback_correct: Catching these signals early gives you the chance to shift and recover rapport before real trust damage occurs.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A sudden drop in engagement is your early warning system. Combined with pressure behaviors, it signals a style mismatch you can still recover from. If you miss it at this stage, you'll have to rebuild trust later. Review Slide 22 for how to spot and act on these signals.
